Capturing When placing a dice, any set of dice which consists of two or more dice all of which or orthogonally adjacent to the dice which was just placed with a total sum of 6 or less eyes in the set of dice can be captured. If there is such a set, the placing player must choose one, remove all the dice in the captured set from the board and set the new dice such as to show the number of eyes that where just removed. If there is no such set, no dice are removed and the new die shows a 1. Game End The game ends when the board has been completely filled. The player with the larger number of dice wins. Cephalopod is a two-player game which employs a 5x5 board, 24 dice of one color, and 24 dice of another color. The board starts out vacant.

Players take turns adding dice of their own color to the board, one die per turn. A newly placed die must show a one, unless it’s a capturing placement, in which case it must show a two or higher. Each player will always have a placement available and must make one. Players cannot pass on their turn.

Once the board has been completely filled, the player whose dice occupy the majority of the squares wins. Draws and ties cannot occur in Cephalopod.

				
				
					Capturing placementIf a die is placed horizontally or vertically adjacent (hereafter “adjacent”) to two dice, and the sum of the pip counts (number of spots on the top surface of a die) on those two adjacent dice is six or less, then the currently played die must show the pip sum of its two adjacent dice, and the player must remove those two adjacent dice from the board immediately, while it is still his turn.

Similarly, if a die is placed adjacent to three or four dice, and if two, three, or four of its adjacent dice have a pip sum of six or less, then two, three, or four of those adjacent dice (whose pip sum is six or less) must be removed, and the played die must show the pip sum of the removed dice.

Captures are mandatory only when placing a die onto a square from which captures are possible.

				
				
					Non-capturing placementA player can make a non-capturing placement simply by adding a die to a square from which no captures are possible. A non-capturing placement must show a single pip.

Players always begin their turn by adding a die. Only dice which are adjacent to the currently added die, and whose pip sum equals the pip count of the currently added die may be removed during the current turn.

[Rating: 2/10] This game is bad. Another game that feels like Tic-Tac-Toe. We played the 3x3 which is MUCH shorter than the 5x5 version, and it still over-stayed its welcome.

[Rating: 3/10] Wow, I really hope there's more going on here than I realize. Like I know if you don't know about the double-cross in Dots-and-Boxes you're going to find it terribly boring. But I found this terribly boring (and [b]long[/b]), and with nothing to speak of in terms of forcing moves, I don't see what could redeem it.  Don't get me wrong, there is certainly skill involved, it [i]is[/i] a game, but if all it involves is look-ahead, you're not [i]making[/i] anything (chains, stacks, cannons, pharisees...) it's going to be a lot harder to hold my interest. [Rating: 4/10] The very fluid board makes it impossible to make heuristic moves and only computational moves.  Not bad design, but not my preference.  Feels like the early game is too evasive -- kind of like 'boxes'.  The board state is brittle, making computation critical but not necessarily interesting.

[Rating: 4/10] There's a nice concept behind this game, and the fact that it's really a free game only adds up points to it.  However, it might be just "too simple". Maybe even easily solvable. I played my first game, and went on and win easily, having grasped much of the game in the first few moves. That's not necessarily a bad thing, but then the game comes to a "lather-rinse-repeat" fashion I simply didn't enjoy.  The first turns a very interesting. [Rating: 4/10] This is one of those Mark Steere games I just "don't get". There's nothing functionally wrong with it; it's just lacking in clarity and fun. I respect it, though.
